content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper proposes a targeted attack on reinforcement learning agents. The goal of the attacker is to add small perturbations masks to an agent’s observations in order to encourage the agent to follow a specific (targeted) set of actions. Each mask corresponds to one specific action, and thus can be thought of as a universal perturbation to induce the agent into taking that specific action. The attack, named CopyCAT, is experimentally compared with current attacks in RL such as the FGSM attack of Huang et al.

I would argue to reject the paper for two key reasons. First, the threat model is not well-motivated or clearly explained. Second, I am not convinced by the soundness of the experimental results because the FGSM baseline seems much worse than it should be. I am also concerned by the lack of ablation studies for the L2 regularization term in the author’s loss function.

The threat model the authors propose is that the attacker should only have read-access to the agent that it wants to attack, and not write-access. In RL terms, this means that the attacker can only attack the current observation, and not the internal state of the agent. However, in the actual experiments, the authors use networks like DQN which take as input 4 frames at a time, and then the authors only apply the mask to the final (4th) state. This seems like a very strange threat model - if an attacker can already attack every 4th state by applying a mask to it, why can’t the attacker just attack every state? In my opinion, the authors should reconsider the threat model, and perhaps focus more on the fact that they are generating universal perturbations for RL agents via action-specific masks, which does seem interesting.

Next, I am worried about the soundness of the experimental results, especially the FGSM baseline. First, in Fig. 4, I do not think the L2 norm of the FGSM-L_inf attack should be on the x-axis - I would not expect the FGSM-L_inf attack to have low L2 norm at all, so it seems unfair to compare something that you explicitly regularize to have low L2 norm (CopyCAT) with something that has no L2 norm constraint.

Second, I do think that it is fair to have FGSM-L2 (I did not see this explicitly discussed anywhere in the text, which should also be addressed, but I assume this is an FGSM attack which is projected to a bounded L2 norm ball) in such a plot. However, it is worrying that the FGSM-L2 attack gets worse as the L2 norm of the allowed perturbation increases. Intuitively, allowing a larger norm attack should make it easier to force the targeted action; as a result, I am worried that the implementation is simply incorrect.

Third, I would like to see ablation studies on the L2 norm regularization term added to CopyCAT. The intuitive explanation for why it was added (we should minimize energy) doesn’t really make much sense to me - why do we want masks of low energy? Couldn’t we just have a separate version of CopyCAT that just does L2 ball projections? Also, in Fig 4., it seems that the attacks with extremely low weight on the L2 norm regularization term perform better, so why have the term at all?

Finally, I am confused why FGSM is so much worse. It seems to me that CopyCAT is very similar to FGSM, but it is computed over an entire training dataset as opposed to for one image. However, I would expect that FGSM on a single datapoint x to result in lower loss on that datapoint than the mask (which maximizes the loss over the whole dataset, not just x). I don’t think it’s a problem if CopyCAT performs slightly worse than FGSM, since the universality of the masks is the interesting feature; I almost think it’s a problem if CopyCAT performs better. If it does indeed perform better, it’s important to figure out which element of CopyCAT makes it perform better.

Some additional feedback:
- In the abstract, you should say what your contributions and results are.
- I think having a section that very clearly outlines the differences (maybe by writing the two algorithms side-by-side) between FGSM and CopyCAT would be immensely helpful for understanding what your contributions are.
- I think having more plots about how the masks transfer to out-of-distribution inputs would be really interesting. For example, you could explicitly start the agent off at states not seen in the data used for training CopyCAT and check if you can still force a specific action using the mask.
- I would also add an additional baseline beyond just DQN vs Rainbow; while the two are different, they are trained to do similar things. I would also consider doing something like Randomly Initialized DQN vs trained DQN, since those have very different goals.

content.title: Re: Official Blind Review #3  (1/2)
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, thank you for your comments. 

"However, in the actual experiments, the authors use networks like DQN which take as input 4 frames at a time, and then the authors only apply the mask to the final (4th) state. This seems like a very strange threat model - if an attacker can already attack every 4th state by applying a mask to it, why can’t the attacker just attack every state?"

        Reinforcement learning handles *sequential* decision problems. The agent uses the last four frames to take a decision at time t, but only observes the last frame and uses the memorized last three frames (stacked in a so-called state). We placed our threat model “at the interface between the agent and the environment where the system is the most vulnerable”. When actually testing the attack (fig1. to 6), we apply it online. We run trajectories and only attack the observation provided by the environment before it is passed to the agent. No change is made to the inner workings of the agent. The attacked observation is passed to the agent and no further intervention is made on the agent. 

In the literature, what we called the state (the four stacked observations) is attacked at every time-step. The last four observations are thus modified at every time step. One observation provided by the environment is thus attacked (and modified in the agent’s memory) several times.
These attacks (as the one from Huang et. al.) cannot be expressed in our threat model with an adversary placed at the interface between the agent and the environment. They require a deeper access to the agent. They require to modify the memory of the agent.
Again, CopyCAT modifies, at each time step, the observation before passing it to the agent. It is, in this sense, much less “invasive”, but this new setting makes the problem harder


"However, it is worrying that the FGSM-L2 attack gets worse as the L2 norm of the allowed perturbation increases. Intuitively, allowing a larger norm attack should make it easier to force the targeted action; as a result, I am worried that the implementation is simply incorrect."

        First we would like to point out that equation (2) explicitly tells what is FGSM-L2. Second, as explained in this same paragraph, FGSM (both L2 and L-inf) are only one single normalized step of gradient. Computing *targeted* adversarial examples is harder than untargeted ones as the attacked network has to find an example leading to a precise label (we highlight that Huang et al, using FGSM, consider only untargeted attacks). 

Increasing epsilon, the allowed norm of FGSM means increasing the step size. As well known in optimization, taking one (and only one) giant step from x in the direction of the gradient computed at x might not a good optimization scheme. That is why optimization-based methods (that take successive steps of gradient) were introduced. And that is why we used such a method.
Once this is clear, another question one may ask is “ then why do you compare only to FGSM, that is a fast but extremely basic method?” We answered this in the paragraph baseline saying that, in sequential decision making, it is not possible to stop the process at each time step to compute a new adversarial example based on an optimization-based method (that is why we developed CopyCAT, which is universal/precomputed). We just compared to the fastest method in the literature, FGSM, that still requires to compute the gradient at each time step while CopyCAT does not.
 To convince you that our FGSM was implemented right, we include another baseline, iterative-FGSM, that takes several steps of gradients and reach the same performance as CopyCAT (but requires several gradient computes at each time step). This experiment can be found in Appendix. B4.


"Why do we want masks of low energy? Couldn’t we just have a separate version of CopyCAT that just does L2 ball projections? Also, in Fig 4., it seems that the attacks with extremely low weight on the L2 norm regularization term perform better, so why have the term at all?"

        The paper deals with targeted attacks against deep RL agents. The used optimization scheme is a choice and indeed, others could be tried.
The objective set by a major part of the adversarial example community is to find small norm adversarial examples (in either L0, L2 or L-inf norms: “Carlini, Nicholas, and David Wagner. "Towards evaluating the robustness of neural networks." 2017 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP). IEEE, 2017.” ). This is true except for certain type of adversarial examples that have not focused on indistinguishable attacks ( “Brown, Tom B., et al. "Adversarial patch." arXiv preprint arXiv:1712.09665 (2017)” ). Having the regularization term helps reducing the L2 norm of the attack and find adversarial examples that are closer to the original observations (and thus less detectable).

(1/2)

content.comment:
"Finally, I am confused why FGSM is so much worse. It seems to me that CopyCAT is very similar to FGSM, but it is computed over an entire training dataset as opposed to for one image. However, I would expect that FGSM on a single datapoint x to result in lower loss on that datapoint than the mask (which maximizes the loss over the whole dataset, not just x). "
		
        As we mentioned before, FGSM is just one single step of gradient while CopyCAT uses a full optimization scheme. It is not surprising that it works much better. What you could expect is that CopyCAT is worse than an iterative method applied at each observation (we did not compare to these classical iterative methods as it would make no sense in a real-time setting). Yet as we explained before, it is not surprising that FGSM is not able to consistently find targeted adversarial examples with a single step of gradient (Eq. 1). Results against an iterative method can be found in the new appendix B4. 


"- In the abstract, you should say what your contributions and results are.
- I think having a section that very clearly outlines the differences (maybe by writing the two algorithms side-by-side) between FGSM and CopyCAT would be immensely helpful for understanding what your contributions are."

	As told in the abstract: "Our main contribution is CopyCAT, a targeted attack able to consistently lure an agent into following an outsider's policy. It is pre-computed, therefore fast inferred, and could thus be usable in a real-time scenario. [...] In [our] setting the adversary cannot directly modify the agent's state -its representation of the environment- but can only attack the agent's observation -its perception of the environment"
 
This sentence sums-up the main difference with the baseline of Huang et. al. Our attack is useable real-time (because it is pre-computed), less invasive (it attacks a single observation rather that the stacked observations we call “state”) and has the more general purpose of making the agent follow another policy rather than just shattering it. 

"I think having more plots about how the masks transfer to out-of-distribution inputs would be really interesting."

        All experiments (fig1, fig2, fig3, fig4, fig5) are done out-of-distribution. Indeed they are tested online, on new states encountered in new trajectories, as explained in the paper (“ Each point of each plot is the average result over 5 policy π seeds and 80 runs for each seed”). What’s more, as we test CopyCAT by attacking with a “better” policy, reaching higher rewards, it brings the agent into states that have never been visited by the agent during training. And still we observed that CopyCAT was generalizing to unseen states (fig.4, fig.5). We also provide new examples in appendix B.3 for more realistic images (on data not used for training CopyCAT).


"I would also add an additional baseline beyond just DQN vs Rainbow; while the two are different, they are trained to do similar things. I would also consider doing something like Randomly Initialized DQN vs trained DQN, since those have very different goals."

	It is indeed an interesting experiment to make and it is now included in Appendix B.1. CopyCat still works well, and FGSM works better in this easier setting (see the discussion in the pdf).

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper tackles the problem of generating more realistic adversarial attacks for neural network policies, that can be generated in real-time and only require altering the current environment observation, not the agent’s state (e.g., saved previous observations). To meet this goal, the proposed approach CopyCAT optimizes for a universal (i.e., input-independent) attack per action, that will lead the attacked policy to output that action.

The evaluations show that CopyCat’s universal attacks are able to measurably alter agents’ behaviour, compared to FGSM attacks. The paper does not compare to more complex, state-of-the-art approaches for generating adversarial examples, because it argues that these approaches take too long to create adversarial examples, which makes them infeasible for real-time attacks. The method used for evaluation is creative -- a policy is attacked to make its actions match those of a *better* policy, and the behaviour of the agent is considered successfully changed if it obtains higher reward than without the attacks.

I found this paper to be well-motivated, and there is a clear contribution here, with the introduction of a universal attack that changes the behavior of neural network policies. However, I have concerns regarding the evaluation, as described below. The writing also needs editing; there are quite a few grammatical errors and confusing / unclear phrasing (e.g., "In the latter" is used incorrectly in a couple places).

Regarding the evaluation, my first concern is that the experiments are all on Atari, in which the visual variation is extremely limited, compared to real-world observations. For instance, most Atari games typically only have a handful of colors. Because of this, I’m not convinced that this approach of generating universal attacks would work on more realistic images, which limits the relevance of this paper.

In addition, it is too strong to claim that showing this approach is effective in the white-box setting means that it will also effective in black-box settings. These universal attacks are computed based on the training observations of the agent. When two agents are trained with deep RL, even if it’s with the same algorithm but with different random initializations of the network, it’s very likely that they will encounter different distributions of states during training. Thus, I would like to see additional experiments that evaluate how this attack performs in the black-box setting.

Finally, there are other approaches that only require a forward pass through a neural network like CopyCAT does, for instance training a generative model to create adversarial attacks (e.g., AdvGAN [1]). Although previous work on this has largely focused on image classification, in essence a policy is just a classifier for which the output is images, so this line of work is worth mentioning and potentially comparing to.

Minor comments / questions:
- It's strange to refer to stacked observations as the "state" of the agent, since typically "state" is instead used to refer to either state features or a learned latent state. So claiming that prior approaches require changing the state of the agent is misleading.
- Why are attacks with smaller l2 norm harder to detect? Is there a citation for this? It seems to me that limiting l-infinity norm is enough to make adversarial examples difficult to detect, and there's no need to limit both l2 and l-infinity. This is an important point, because the evaluations compare algorithms with respect to l2 norm.
- Section 4 (Related Work) should be placed earlier in the paper, ideally right after the Introduction.
- Regarding reproducibility -- where were the DQN and Rainbow agents obtained from? If they were trained in-house, what architecture and learning hyperparameters were used?

[1] C. Xiao, B. Li, J. Zhu, W. He, M. Liu, D. Song. Generating Adversarial Examples with Adversarial Networks. IJCAI 2018.

content.title: Re: Official Blind Review #1
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, thank you for your comments. 

"The writing also needs editing."
        We are happy to correct the errors you mentioned and to proofread the paper again.


"Regarding the evaluation, my first concern is that the experiments are all on Atari, in which the visual variation is extremely limited, compared to real-world observations. For instance, most Atari games typically only have a handful of colors. Because of this, I’m not convinced that this approach of generating universal attacks would work on more realistic images, which limits the relevance of this paper."

        The goal of the paper was to enlighten vulnerabilities of reinforcement learning agents. For discrete actions domains, Atari remains a standard benchmark. Reinforcement learning does not yet solve realistic-image based environments, and we need agents that actually work before starting to attack them. 
Regarding the existence of universal adversarial examples for more realistic image manifolds, we want to point out that it was shown in “Brown, Tom B., et al. "Adversarial patch." arXiv preprint arXiv:1712.09665 (2017)”  that it was indeed possible to compute universal adversarial examples on ImageNet. However they did not define their attack as an additional mask.
We thus ran some experiments on ImageNet using the proposed CopyCat approach and observed the existence of universal adversarial additional masks on ImageNet, generalizing to unseen images. 
We show this experiment in the new Appendix B.3.


"When two agents are trained with deep RL, even if it’s with the same algorithm but with different random initializations of the network, it’s very likely that they will encounter different distributions of states during training. Thus, I would like to see additional experiments that evaluate how this attack performs in the black-box setting.

        The black-box setting is is indeed a very interesting problem. Even in the supervised learning setting, it is not solved yet, particularly for targeted adversarial examples (see Liu, Yanpei, et al. "Delving into transferable adversarial examples and black-box attacks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1611.02770 (2016).).
Although this area has not been explored a lot yet, we would like to share with you some preliminary results we have in the black-box setting you describe, where the adversary has no access to the agent’s weights but only to other agents trained with the same algorithms. These results are shown in the new Appendix B.2.


"Finally, there are other approaches that only require a forward pass through a neural network like CopyCAT does, for instance training a generative model to create adversarial attacks (e.g., AdvGAN [1])."

        Indeed, we shall probably cite the paper in the background however it is not a “bounded” attack, it is thus hard to compare fairly to it. We kindly remind that the contribution was a very “simple” attack (only one mask per action) and that it is a new approach to the best of our knowledge. Yet, this is an interesting direction for future work, thanks.


"It's strange to refer to stacked observations as the "state" of the agent."

        We understand your concern and we added a sentence to explicitly tell what we call the state. 
Yet in Markov Decision Processes, an agent, given the current state, takes an action. It gets in return a new state and a reward. In Atari, frames given by the environment are called observations because they do not ensure the Markov property (e.g. in Pong, given an observation, that is a single frame, one cannot know if the ball is going left or right). That is why most algorithms on Atari build a state as a stack of four observations (this way, in Pong, the Markov property is ensured and given a state, one can know if the ball is going left or right). We call “state” the actual input of the neural network approximating the policy.
Indeed the word “state” is also used by the GAN/VAE community (and more generally deep learning) to talk about the latent space computed by the deep network. However, we argue that in the context of Reinforcement Learning, calling “state” the “augmented observation” the agent builds to try to ensure the Markov property is not wrong.


"Why are attacks with smaller l2 norm harder to detect?"

	In finite dimension, norms are equivalent so smaller L2 norm attacks are harder to detect for the same reason small L-inf norm attacks are harder to attack. Small norm attacks are harder to detect as they let the attacked image closer to the original one.

content.review:
This paper develops a RL attack algorithm named CopyCAT, which can lure a policy into a desired behavior  with a finite set of additive masks. The experiments on Atari games validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Despite the previous works in RL attack, I feel CopyCAT is impressive in the potential of running in real time and taking control of a neural policy. However, I still want to see some comparisons with previous works in the experiments. With real examples we can understand the solutions better. 

Detailed comments:
- Figure 1: I cannot see which curve stands for CopyCAT
- Figure 6: hard to read

content.title: Re: Official Blind Review #2
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, thank you for your comments. 

"However, I still want to see some comparisons with previous works in the experiments:"

        Few previous work tackled the issue of targeted attacks in reinforcement learning. As far as we know, we are the only ones to address  this more realistic setting we propose (real-time and observation-only attacks). We thus adapted the paper from Huang et. al. --that uses untargeted FGSM against deep RL policies-- to our targeted realistic setting. This is straightforward and this is was we used as a baseline to compare our algorithm.

"With real examples we can understand the solutions better."

        We are not sure what you mean by “real examples”. Can you please clarify the question? A video showing an attack the can be found at this anonymized link. In this video, the additional mask corresponding to one specific action is constantly applied. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r6FegERfEI0 (in the video, the shown attack has no constraint on epsilon). Moreover, the Atari games we consider are representative of the complexity of an environment that current reinforcement learning agents can address.

"Figure 1: I cannot see which curve stands for CopyCAT"

        As told in the paragraph above Fig. 1 and shown in the legend, dashed lines correspond to FGSM and plain curves stand for CopyCAT. Colors give the value of the bound on the L-inf norm of the attack. The L2-norm of the corresponding attack is plotted against the used regularization parameter.

"Figure 6: hard to read"

        This figure is here to help the reader visualize the attack. On the left, you can see the unattacked observation. On the right, the CopyCAT attack for the action ‘no-op’. In the middle, the attacked observation (left+right). Below is written the action the same DQN network takes in the given situation.
